title: Showing Up Is a Form of Speech
excerpt: Civic life doesn’t start on election day. It starts when you decide your voice belongs in the room.
imageAlt: US Capitol dome against a clear sky
content:
Politics can feel like something that happens *to* you — a feed of headlines, a scroll of outrage, a cycle that never asks you to step in.

I started writing here because I believe awareness is active. Paying attention is a choice. Sharing what you’re learning is a choice. Reaching out to someone who disagrees with you — carefully, honestly — is a choice.

**Showing up** doesn’t always mean a protest sign or a podium. Sometimes it means reading past the headline. Sometimes it means asking a harder question at dinner. Sometimes it means posting when silence would be easier.

This space is for that kind of showing up: personal, curious, and unfinished on purpose.

title: Soft Power, Hard Truths
excerpt: Feminism isn’t a vibe — it’s the daily work of noticing who gets heard, hired, believed, and believed in.
imageAlt: Supreme Court building facade in Washington DC
content:
There’s a version of feminism that looks great on a mood board and another that lives in policy, paychecks, and who gets interrupted in meetings.

I’m interested in both the aesthetic and the substance — the posters *and* the practice. Equality isn’t soft just because it wears a clean outfit. It’s disciplined. It’s specific. It asks who is missing from the table and why.

If you’re building a career, a campus community, or a public voice, you don’t need permission to care about this. You need clarity, courage, and people who will tell you the truth when the room gets comfortable.

This is one of the threads I’ll keep pulling here: how personal growth and public life braid together for women who want more than a seat — who want a say.

title: Equality Isn’t Optional Civic Literacy
excerpt: Racial justice isn’t a side topic. It’s the test of whether our institutions mean what they say.
imageAlt: American flag detail in soft light
content:
If you’re learning politics in real time — through classes, internships, feeds, or late-night conversations — you eventually hit a fork: treat equality as optional enrichment, or treat it as core civic literacy.

I choose the second.

Racial equality isn’t a trend board or a once-a-year post. It’s how we measure whether democracy is actually delivering. It’s who feels safe walking home. Who gets the benefit of the doubt. Who gets to imagine a future in the same city as everyone else.

I’m not here with a finished manifesto. I’m here documenting the learning — linking what I read, what I notice in DC, and what I’m still wrestling with. If that resonates, stick around. If you have something to teach me, reach out.

title: The District as Classroom
excerpt: Monuments are beautiful. The metro at rush hour teaches you just as much about power, access, and who this city is for.
content:
Washington looks like a postcard until you live inside it.

The Capitol dome at dusk, the Lincoln steps, Georgetown brick — that’s the mood board. Then there’s the metro at 8:12 a.m., the intern badge lines, the hearings you watch on your phone between classes, the quiet realization that policy is made by people who also buy coffee and miss trains.

I want this account — and this site — to hold both: the romance of civic ambition **and** the unglamorous work of staying informed.

If you’re in the District, or dreaming of it, or watching from somewhere else entirely: you’re part of the audience I’m writing for. Awareness travels. Connections do too.

title: Reach Out Before You Burn Out
excerpt: Personal growth in public life isn’t a solo grind. Connection is the strategy.
imageAlt: Jefferson Memorial across the Tidal Basin
content:
Spreading awareness without community is a fast way to feel loud and alone.

I’m building in public because I want conversations — with peers, mentors, organizers, classmates, strangers who care about the same fights. Posts are invitations, not performances.

If something here sparks a thought, disagree productively. Share it with someone who should see it. Or just say hello.

Growth doesn’t only happen in silence with a book. Sometimes it happens when you send the first message.
